title: SG-3.4 Hypothesis Testing with Normal Data

3.4.1.examLens: Choose between the 1-sample, 2-sample, and paired t-test, compute the statistic by hand, and compare it to the t table.

worked.question: Nine operators are timed on a task before and after training. The differences (before minus after) have mean d̄ = 2.5 minutes and standard deviation s_d = 3.0. (a) Which test? (b) Compute t and decide at α = 0.05, two-sided. (c) Build the 95% confidence interval for the mean improvement.
worked.solution:
(a) The same people are measured twice, so use the paired t-test.
(b) SE = 3.0 ÷ √9 = 1.0. t = 2.5 ÷ 1.0 = 2.5, with df = 8. The critical value is 2.306. Since 2.5 exceeds 2.306, reject H0: the training changed the mean time.
(c) 2.5 ± 2.306 × 1.0 = 0.19 to 4.81 minutes. The interval excludes zero, which agrees with the test. The interval is wide, so the improvement could be small.

3.4.2.examLens: When the question is about variation (not the average), use a variance test. Read the χ² and F tables correctly.

worked.question: (a) A process standard deviation target is 4. A sample of 16 has s = 5.2. Is the variation higher than target at α = 0.05? (b) Two lines have s1 = 4.0 (n = 11) and s2 = 2.5 (n = 13). Is line 1 more variable?
worked.solution:
(a) χ² = 15 × 5.2² ÷ 4² = 15 × 27.04 ÷ 16 = 25.35. The 0.05 upper critical value at df = 15 is 24.996. Reject H0: variation exceeds the target (the margin is thin).
(b) F = 4.0² ÷ 2.5² = 2.56, df (10, 12), critical 2.75. Fail to reject. There is not enough evidence that line 1 is more variable.

3.4.3.examLens: Complete an ANOVA table, read the F table, interpret a p-value, and know what to do after a significant result. The reference sheet gives the sums-of-squares formulas but not the df, MS, or F.

worked.question:
Three machines, four parts each:

  • A: 10, 12, 11, 13
  • B: 14, 15, 13, 14
  • C: 11, 10, 12, 11

Complete the ANOVA at α = 0.05.
worked.solution:
Totals: T(A) = 46, T(B) = 56, T(C) = 44, grand total T = 146, N = 12.
C = 146² ÷ 12 = 21,316 ÷ 12 = 1,776.33.
ΣX² = (100 + 144 + 121 + 169) + (196 + 225 + 169 + 196) + (121 + 100 + 144 + 121) = 534 + 786 + 486 = 1,806.
SS total = 1,806 − 1,776.33 = 29.67.
SS treatment = (46² + 56² + 44²) ÷ 4 − C = 7,188 ÷ 4 − 1,776.33 = 1,797 − 1,776.33 = 20.67.
SS error = 29.67 − 20.67 = 9.00.

SourceSSdfMSF
Machine (between)20.67210.3310.33
Error (within)9.0091.00
Total29.6711

The F table for df (2, 9) gives 4.26. Since 10.33 exceeds 4.26, reject H0: at least one machine mean differs. A post-hoc test would likely single out machine B (mean 14.0) against A (11.5) and C (11.0).

3.4.1.a.title: The 1-sample t-test
3.4.1.a.html:
t = (x̄ − μ0) ÷ (s ÷ √n), with df = n − 1. It compares one sample mean to a target value μ0.
Example: n = 9, x̄ = 12.5, μ0 = 12, s = 0.9. SE = 0.9 ÷ 3 = 0.3. t = 0.5 ÷ 0.3 = 1.67. For df = 8 the two-tailed critical value (0.975 column) is 2.306. Since 1.67 is below 2.306, fail to reject H0.

3.4.1.b.title: The 2-sample t-test
3.4.1.b.html:
t = (x̄1 − x̄2) ÷ √( s1²/n1 + s2²/n2 ) (the Welch version, which does not assume equal variances). The pooled version assumes equal variances.
Example: group 1: x̄ = 20.0, s = 2, n = 10. Group 2: x̄ = 22.0, s = 3, n = 12. s1²/n1 = 0.40, s2²/n2 = 0.75. SE = √1.15 = 1.072. t = −2.0 ÷ 1.072 = −1.87. Welch df ≈ 19, critical value 2.093. Since 1.87 is below 2.093, fail to reject H0.

3.4.1.c.title: The paired t-test
3.4.1.c.html: t = d̄ ÷ (s_d ÷ √n), where d is the difference within each pair, n is the number of pairs, and df = n − 1. Pairing removes unit-to-unit variation, which makes the test more sensitive.

3.4.1.d.title: Assumptions
3.4.1.d.html:
• The observations are independent.
  • The data (or the differences, for a paired test) are approximately normal, which matters most with small samples.
  • The pooled t-test also needs equal variances. The Welch version does not.

3.4.1.e.title: Interpreting the result
3.4.1.e.html: Report the p-value and the confidence interval for the difference. If the interval excludes zero, the means differ. Always translate the result back to the practical question.

3.4.1.f.title: The Z-test
3.4.1.f.html: Extension. When the population σ is known, use a z-test: z = (x̄ − μ0) ÷ (σ ÷ √n). In practice σ is rarely known.

3.4.1.g.title: Paired or 2-sample?
3.4.1.g.html: Before and after on the same units, or matched pairs, means paired. Two separate groups means 2-sample. Using the wrong one is the most common error on this topic.

3.4.1.h.title: The reference-sheet versions
3.4.1.h.html:
• Welch df = (A + B)² ÷ [ A² ÷ (n1 − 1) + B² ÷ (n2 − 1) ], where A = s1²/n1 and B = s2²/n2.
  • Pooled s_p = √{ [ (n1 − 1)s1² + (n2 − 1)s2² ] ÷ (n1 + n2 − 2) }. For the pooled t-test, df = n1 + n2 − 2.
  • 2-sample Z is used when the population σ's are known.

The sheet's subscripts show "n − 1" generically, so always use the df that matches the test.

3.4.2.a.title: The chi-square test for a variance
3.4.2.a.html:
χ² = (n − 1) × s² ÷ σ0², with df = n − 1. It compares a sample variance to a target variance σ0².
Example: the target σ0 = 4. A sample of n = 16 has s = 5.2. χ² = 15 × 27.04 ÷ 16 = 25.35. For df = 15, the upper 0.05 critical value is 24.996. Since 25.35 exceeds it, reject H0 and conclude the variation exceeds the target (one-sided test).

3.4.2.b.title: What it tests
3.4.2.b.html: Whether the process variation is different from, greater than, or less than a target. Variance questions are about consistency, not the average.

3.4.2.c.title: Sensitivity to non-normality
3.4.2.c.html: The χ² test for a variance is very sensitive to departures from normality. Check normality first.

3.4.2.d.title: Comparing two variances
3.4.2.d.html: F = s1² ÷ s2². Levene's test is the version that is robust to non-normality.

3.4.2.e.title: "Did variation decrease?"
3.4.2.e.html: That is a variance test, not a mean test. A change in the average tells you nothing about consistency.

3.4.2.f.title: The F test for two variances
3.4.2.f.html:
F = s1² ÷ s2², with df (n1 − 1, n2 − 1). Put the larger variance in the numerator. The reference sheet also shows a confidence interval for the ratio of variances using F values in both directions.
Example: s1 = 4.0 (n1 = 11), s2 = 2.5 (n2 = 13). F = 16 ÷ 6.25 = 2.56, df = (10, 12). The F table (α = 0.05, one-sided) gives 2.75. Since 2.56 is below 2.75, fail to reject H0.

3.4.2.g.title: Reading the χ² table
3.4.2.g.html:
The χ² table gives right-tail probabilities. Table 1 has columns 0.250 down to 0.001. Table 2 has columns 0.995 down to 0.500. Rows are df 1 to 30, then 40 to 100 by 10.
For a two-sided variance test use both ends: the α/2 column for the upper critical value and the 1 − α/2 column for the lower.
Example: df = 15, α = 0.05 two-sided. Upper critical (0.025 column) = 27.488. Lower critical (0.975 column) = 6.262. Reject H0 if χ² falls below 6.262 or above 27.488.

3.4.3.a.title: The hypotheses
3.4.3.a.html: H0: all the means are equal. Ha: at least one mean differs. ANOVA compares three or more group means.

3.4.3.b.title: Why not several t-tests?
3.4.3.b.html: Each test carries its own α risk, and the risks add up. With three groups (three pairwise tests) at α = 0.05, the chance of at least one false alarm is about 1 − 0.95³ = 14%. ANOVA keeps the overall risk at α.

3.4.3.c.title: The ANOVA relationships
3.4.3.c.html:
• SS total = SS between (treatment) + SS within (error).
  • MS = SS ÷ df.
  • F = MS between ÷ MS within.

A large F means the group means differ by more than the noise within the groups would explain.

3.4.3.d.title: Degrees of freedom
3.4.3.d.html:
With k groups and N observations in total:

  • df between = k − 1
  • df within = N − k
  • df total = N − 1

3.4.3.e.title: Assumptions
3.4.3.e.html: Independent observations, normal residuals, and equal variances across groups (check with Levene's or Bartlett's test).

3.4.3.f.title: After a significant result
3.4.3.f.html: ANOVA says "at least one differs," not which. Use a post-hoc comparison (Tukey, Fisher, or Dunnett against a control) or an interval plot to find the differences.

3.4.3.g.title: What the topic includes
3.4.3.g.html: Equal-variance tests, normality tests, sample-size calculation, and reading ANOVA output.

3.4.3.h.title: Fill in a missing cell
3.4.3.h.html: Use the relationships above. Given SS between = 40 (df 3) and SS within = 80 (df 16): MS between = 13.33, MS within = 5.00, F = 2.67. The F table (α = 0.05, df 3 and 16) gives 3.24, so fail to reject. Then name the next step (if significant, a post-hoc test).

3.4.3.i.title: Bartlett versus Levene
3.4.3.i.html: Bartlett's test assumes the data are normal. Levene's test is robust to non-normality. If normality is doubtful, use Levene's.

3.4.3.j.title: Do not name a winner
3.4.3.j.html: A significant ANOVA means at least one mean differs. Do not declare the largest sample mean "the best" without post-hoc evidence. In Tukey or Fisher pairwise intervals, an interval that contains 0 means no evidence of a difference for that pair.

3.4.3.k.title: Sample size and power for ANOVA
3.4.3.k.html: The inputs are the number of levels, the smallest difference between means worth detecting, σ, α, and the power you want. Smaller differences and larger σ need more data.

3.4.3.l.title: Reading the F table
3.4.3.l.html:
The F tables in the reference document give upper-tail critical values for α = 0.05, α = 0.01, and α = 0.10, each in two parts (columns 1 to 10, then 12 to infinity).

  • Columns are the numerator df: 1 to 10, then 12, 15, 20, 24, 30, 40, 60, 120, ∞.
  • Rows are the denominator df.
  • The ANOVA F test is upper-tailed, so α = 0.05 works directly.
  • For a two-sided variance test, put the larger variance in the numerator. The α = 0.05 table then corresponds to a two-sided test at α = 0.10, and the α = 0.01 table to α = 0.02. There is no α = 0.025 table, so a two-sided test at exactly 0.05 cannot be read from the sheet.

Examples: df (2, 9) gives 4.26. df (3, 16) gives 3.24. df (10, 12) gives 2.75.

3.4.3.m.title: ANOVA by hand with the reference-sheet formulas
3.4.3.m.html:
• C = T² ÷ N, the correction factor (T is the grand total of all data).
  • SS total = ΣX² − (ΣX)² ÷ N, which equals ΣX² − C. It also equals (N − 1) × s² of all data.
  • SS treatment = Σ(Tᵢ² ÷ nᵢ) − C, where Tᵢ is the total of group i. Equivalent forms: Σnᵢ·X̄ᵢ² − N·X̿², or for equal group sizes n(k − 1) × s² of the group means.
  • SS error = SS total − SS treatment.

3.4.3.n.title: What is not on the sheet
3.4.3.n.html: The sheet does not give df (k − 1, N − k, N − 1), MS = SS ÷ df, or F = MS treatment ÷ MS error. Know them.

3.4.1-1.stem: A sample of 16 has a mean of 52 and a standard deviation of 6. Test H0: μ = 50 against Ha: μ not equal to 50. What is the decision?

options.html: Fail to reject H0, since t = 1.33 is below the critical value of 2.131
Fail to reject H0, since t = 0.33

3.4.1-1.explanation: t = (52 − 50) ÷ (6 ÷ √16) = 2 ÷ 1.5 = 1.33. With df = 15 the two-tailed critical value is 2.131, so fail to reject.

3.4.1-2.stem: Two independent groups each have n = 10 and s = 4. The means are 30 and 26. Using the pooled t-test, what is the decision?

options.html: Fail to reject H0, since t = 1.12
Reject H0, since t = 2.24 exceeds the critical value of 2.101
Fail to reject H0, since t = 2.24 is below 2.101

3.4.1-2.explanation: s_p = 4. SE = 4 × √(1/10 + 1/10) = 1.789. t = 4 ÷ 1.789 = 2.24. With df = 18 the critical value is 2.101, so reject H0.

3.4.1-3.stem: Sixteen operators are timed before and after training. The mean difference is 1.5 minutes with a standard deviation of the differences of 2.0. What is the decision for a two-sided test?

options.html: Fail to reject H0, since t = 0.75
Reject H0, since t = 3.0 exceeds the critical value of 2.131
Fail to reject H0, since t = 3.0 is below 2.131

3.4.1-3.explanation: t = 1.5 ÷ (2.0 ÷ √16) = 1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 3.0. With df = 15, the critical value is 2.131, so reject H0.

3.4.1-4.stem: Two inspectors each measure the same 20 parts. A team wants to know whether their average readings differ. Which test fits?
3.4.1-4.explanation: The same parts are measured by both inspectors, so the data are paired.

3.4.1-5.stem: Which version of the 2-sample t-test does NOT assume equal variances?
3.4.1-5.explanation: Welch's version uses each sample's own variance and an adjusted df.

3.4.2-1.stem: A target standard deviation is 2. A sample of 21 has s = 3. Test whether the variation exceeds the target (one-sided, α = 0.05). The upper 0.05 χ² critical value for df = 20 is 31.410. What is the conclusion?

options.html: Fail to reject H0, since χ² = 13.3
Fail to reject H0, since χ² = 45 is below 31.410

3.4.2-1.explanation: χ² = (n − 1)s² ÷ σ0² = 20 × 9 ÷ 4 = 45, which exceeds 31.410. The variation is greater than the target.

3.4.2-2.stem: Sample 1 has s² = 9 (n = 9) and sample 2 has s² = 4 (n = 11). The one-sided F critical value at α = 0.05 for df (8, 10) is 3.07. What is the conclusion?

options.html: Fail to reject H0, since F = 2.25 is below 3.07
Fail to reject H0, since F = 0.44

3.4.2-2.explanation: F = 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25 (larger variance on top). It is below 3.07, so there is not enough evidence that the variances differ.

3.4.2-3.stem: The chi-square test for a single variance is robust to departures from normality.
3.4.2-3.explanation: It is very sensitive to non-normality, so check normality first.

3.4.3-1.stem: An ANOVA has SS between = 60 with 2 df, and SS within = 108 with 18 df. The α = 0.05 critical F for df (2, 18) is 3.55. What is F, and what is the decision?
3.4.3-1.explanation: MS between = 60 ÷ 2 = 30. MS within = 108 ÷ 18 = 6. F = 30 ÷ 6 = 5.0, which exceeds 3.55. At least one mean differs.

3.4.3-2.stem: A one-way ANOVA compares k = 4 groups with N = 24 observations in total. What are the degrees of freedom between groups and within groups?
3.4.3-2.explanation: df between = k − 1 = 3. df within = N − k = 20. (Total is N − 1 = 23.)

3.4.3-3.stem: Why is one-way ANOVA preferred over running several t-tests on the same groups?

options.html: Several t-tests inflate the overall chance of a false alarm, while ANOVA controls it

3.4.3-3.explanation: Each additional test adds its own α risk. With three groups at α = 0.05, the chance of at least one false alarm is about 14%.

3.4.3-4.stem: A significant ANOVA shows that the group with the highest sample mean is the best group.
3.4.3-4.explanation: A significant ANOVA only says at least one mean differs. A post-hoc comparison is needed to say which groups differ.

3.4.3-5.stem: Three machines each produce 4 parts. The totals are 46, 56, and 44, so the grand total is 146 and N = 12. Using the correction factor C = T² ÷ N = 1,776.33, what is SS treatment, using SS = Σ(Tᵢ² ÷ nᵢ) − C?

3.4.3-6.stem: Group data may not be normal and a team needs to check whether the variances are equal before ANOVA. Which test is robust to non-normality?
3.4.3-6.explanation: Levene's test does not require normal data. Bartlett's does.

3.4.3-7.text: A one-way ANOVA has k = 3 groups and N = 18 observations. Give the degrees of freedom between, within, and total.
3.4.3-7.answer: Between = k − 1 = 2. Within = N − k = 15. Total = N − 1 = 17.
